title: Probability
description: The probability scale, calculating simple probabilities, sample spaces, and experimental vs theoretical probability.

notes.heading: The Probability Scale
notes.body: Probability is a number between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain). 0.5 = equally likely as not. Can be written as fraction, decimal, or percentage: 1/4 = 0.25 = 25%. The probability scale: 0 = impossible, 1 = certain, everything in between measures likelihood.

notes.heading: Calculating Probability
notes.body: P(event) = favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes. Example: bag with 3 red, 5 blue, 2 green marbles: P(red)=3/10=0.3. All probabilities sum to 1. P(not event) = 1 − P(event). All probabilities must be between 0 and 1.

notes.heading: Sample Spaces
notes.body: The set of ALL possible outcomes. For a die: {1,2,3,4,5,6}. For two coins: {HH, HT, TH, TT} — 4 equally likely outcomes with P=1/4 each. Use a table for two dice (36 outcomes). Always check: do all outcomes sum to the total? Are they equally likely?

notes.heading: Experimental vs Theoretical
notes.body: Theoretical = what SHOULD happen (favourable ÷ total). Experimental (relative frequency) = what ACTUALLY happens (occurrences ÷ trials). Example: 100 coin flips, 47 heads → experimental P=0.47, theoretical P=0.5. More trials → experimental gets closer to theoretical (law of large numbers).

notes.heading: ⚠️ Equally likely outcomes
notes.body: A probability calculation only works if every outcome is equally likely. A spinner with a bigger red section gives red a higher chance than blue. Always ask, 'Are all outcomes fair?' before using P = favourable ÷ total.

notes.heading: ✅ Listing without missing outcomes
notes.body: Use a table or tree diagram so you do not miss any outcomes. For two coins, listing HH, HT, TH, TT is better than just saying "2 heads, 1 head, no heads" because those groups are not equally likely.

questions.explanation: 11 letters total, B appears twice. P=2/11.

questions.stem: A class has 14 girls and 16 boys. One student is chosen at random. What is the probability it is a girl?
questions.explanation: Total students = 14 + 16 = 30. Number of girls = 14. P(girl) = 14/30 = 7/15 when simplified.

questions.stem: A fair coin is tossed twice. Is getting two heads equally likely as getting one head and one tail?
choices: No — one head and one tail has two ways to happen
No — two heads is more likely
questions.explanation: Sample space: HH, HT, TH, TT. P(two heads)=1/4. P(one head and one tail)=2/4=1/2 because HT and TH are different outcomes.

questions.stem: Two dice are rolled and the scores are added. What is the probability of getting a total of 7?
questions.explanation: There are 36 equally likely outcomes. Totals of 7 can be made by (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1) — 6 ways. P(7)=6/36=1/6.
